As a corollary, that minimizes the amount of thermal insulation that must be installed on the tank surface, minimizing initial and future maintenance costs. Finally, spheres can be expected to take up significantly less land area for a given storage volume compared to horizontally oriented bullet tanks. In Figure 4.28, the land area required for 11 bullet tanks of 30,000 m3 combined capacity is overlayed on the land area required for four spheres of equal combined capacity. The four spheres require approximately half the land area of the bullets. This can be a major advantage when available land area is a challenge and local height restrictions are not an issue. The major disadvantage to spherical tanks is that they generally must be assembled on site due to their size. In this configuration they would be too large to transport from a fabrication shop to the site intact. See Figure 4.29 which shows a spherical tank under construction, approximately the same size as has been proposed for the T-RICH site. On site fabrication can be a disadvantage for two reasons. First, it is likely to be more expensive to build the tanks onsite in Tampa using a crew of workers from the tank manufacturer’s home base which may be several states away. Such workers will incur increased temporary housing costs (i.e. hotels) and may incur additional pay due to being away from home. Indeed, a budgetary quotation received for four spherical tanks, built onsite, was approximately 50% greater than a quote for tanks built overseas by a tank manufacturer that has already built CO tanks for European 2 projects. Second, quality control of tank fabrication can be expected to be marginally lower onsite compared to the tank maker’s home facility where a more controlled fabrication environment is possible. Figure 4.28: Comparison of Land Area Required by Horizontal Bullet Tanks and Spherical Tanks Page90 of158 T-RICH Pre-FEED Report – Public Version Figure 4.29: Typical Spherical Tank Under Construction (source: American Tank & Vessel) 4.9.2 COOLING OPTIONS The high ambient temperature in Tampa will make air cooling less effective than in more temperate climates. This in turn drives liquefaction compressor interstage temperatures upwards and increases total motor loads. Seawater (or freshwater) cooling may offer advantages over air cooling by eliminating noisy forced draft air exchangers and potentially allowing for closer temperature approaches. However, the EPA has specific regulations (62-302.520 Thermal Surface Water Criteria) regarding the use of seawater in this location. These regulations state that the surface temperature of the receiving body of water must not be raised above 97ºF (36ºC). Utilizing seawater as a cooling medium for the interstage coolers would require large heat exchangers made from titanium materials, which would add complexity to the plant. This option was not progressed further during Pre-FEED, however it can be revisited during later design phases.
